title: God's words to Job as a gift after victory
english: Let us remember this saying as useful whenever God judges that we should suffer something: to lose a child, to lose a position, to fall ill in body, or to undergo anything whatever of this kind. None of these things can happen to us unless God judges it. Since, then, none of these things occurs without God's judgment, the one who suffers is told, “Do not reject my judgment” (Job 40:8). That is, do not deny what I have judged concerning you; he means the present oracle. God says to him, “Do you think I have dealt with you for any other reason than that you might be revealed as righteous? I make my defense to you: you were righteous, but you were not seen to be so. You had endurance, but I needed to provide an occasion for your endurance to shine. You had courage, but it was hidden within you; the pains that befell you displayed your courage.”

Let us remember these things in times of adversity, and we will seem to hear God present and saying to us, “Do you think I have dealt with you for any other reason”—that is, permitted the trial—“than that your righteousness might be clear to those who do not know it? Take up your height.”

The verses can also be understood this way: You have conquered the tempter; take up your height. Take up your power. Be crowned. Clothe yourself in splendor. The arrogant one marched against you, but you humbled the proud one and turned him back far off in shame with his whole host.

orientation: Origen is expounding God's address to Job after his trials, explaining that every suffering comes by God's judgment and that God's questions to Job are meant to reveal his hidden virtues.

title: The dragon bound and given as food; the saint examines the dragon's folds; the dragon's eyes imitate the morning star
english: It describes the end of a great, strong, and perfect soul, because the dragon has been handed over to him like a sparrow to a child, unable even to harm the child, since the child can lead it bound wherever he wishes and carry it about; so by the Lord's grace Satan has become bound like a sparrow in the hands of infants and sucklings, from whose mouth God has prepared praise (Psalm 8:2). Nations are fed on him. Just as the Lord is food for the faithful, so the dragon is food for the ungodly; 'You gave him as food to the peoples, the Ethiopians' (Psalm 74:14)—that is, to the children of darkness, to those in ignorance. For with every word we receive, we either eat from the dragon if we accept a vain hearing, or from Christ if we accept a word that builds up and benefits.

No ship, though they gather together, will ever bear one hide of his tail. To speak more plainly: human beings, who use their bodies as ships, cannot by themselves mortify the tail of the dragon and its final parts; but with divine power overseeing, we can bring the whole of him and mortify it. Each of us mortifies the devil, so far as lies in himself, according to the word: 'And God will crush Satan under your feet quickly' (Romans 16:20). Who would enter a fold of his breast? The breast and the chest are named as the place where the ruling part is. His breast is not simple; it is deceitful, it is folded. A holy person can convict him and show that it is folded; for to the holy one it is not folded. And a spirit shall not pass through him. The words 'shall not pass through' do not mean that it does not go through and pass by, but that nothing escapes him; all must come through him. Let us therefore prepare ourselves, so as not to be seized by him. His eyes have the appearance of the morning star.

orientation: Origen continues interpreting Job 41, showing how the dragon (Satan) is delivered bound like a sparrow to simple believers, becomes food for the ungodly, and is mortified by divine power; he then examines the dragon's folded breast as the seat of deceit and notes that no spirit passes through him unperceived, ending with the dragon's eyes having the appearance of the morning star.

title: The dragon's eyes, mouth, and forerunner destruction
english: His eyes, then, are not morning stars, but "the appearance of a morning star" (Job 41:18), for he transforms himself into an angel of light (2 Corinthians 11:14). He pretends to be a heavenly star; he pretends to be a sign of day. "Like burning lamps" (Job 41:19). I think that all the impious introducers of godless doctrines are the mouth of the dragon. But something may also be understood figuratively from this, from which destructive words come. If you have ever heard a word that, under the pretext of Christianity, accuses the Creator—say, one that advocates the doctrines of Marcion, of Valentinus, of Basilides—when they speak evil of the Maker of heaven and earth, when they say anything similar, you will see that firebrands come out of the mouth of such people. Let us guard ourselves, then, lest those lamps burn us; lest the hearths of fire touch us. "Destruction runs before him" (Job 41:22). Destruction is like a forerunner to him and serves as his bodyguard. Wherever he is about to come, his destruction runs ahead, and only then does he enter. If a person does not first welcome destruction, he does not welcome the dragon. For when someone sins, then, having itching ears, he seeks teachers, being destroyed; and seeking teachers, after being destroyed he finds the dragon and welcomes into his own soul the dragon, filled with so many evils.

Chapter 42. "And the Lord gave double" (Job 42:10). The one who has endured every trial receives as prizes of his endurance all things double compared to before. But the Lord gives prizes not only doubled, but a hundredfold. And he would not have received double of his former things if he had not displayed double the virtue.
